newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Economists look for revisions in NZ GDP series.
newsitem.headline: Economists look for revisions in NZ GDP series.

text.p: New Zealand financial markets are unlikely to move when September quarter GDP figures are released on Thursday, but economists say there may be significant upward growth revisions to past quarters.
"The most interesting thing will be the revisions," said David Plank, chief economist at Bankers Trust New Zealand. "History will be revised upwards significantly."

He said Statistics New Zealand had already released some data for expenditure to GDP which showed an upward revision to personal consumption, and nominal data for the March year also pointed to an upward revision.
"So if the year to March gets revised up significantly, maybe by half a percent to a percent in annual terms...then the slowdown (since then) looks sharper than it did before.
"That's bullish for the easing story," Plank said.

Monetary conditions were now tighter than the Reserve Bank had assumed in its December Monetary Policy statement because of the recent appreciation in the New Zealand dollar, leaving scope for some easing in conditions.

"We'll have had higher growth than we thought, but we've had the same inflation, so your previous growth/inflation trade-offs look better, and now we've got growth slowing faster than we thought," Plank said.

Economists polled by Reuters on average expect a seasonally adjusted 0.21 percent rise in production-based GDP in the September quarter. They see 1.72 percent point-to-point growth between the September 1995 and September 1996 quarters, and average actual GDP growth of 2.25 percent for the year.
However, with the slowdown in economic growth expected to bottom out in December and a pick-up in activity seen in March, the GDP statistics for those quarters would be of greater significance.

"The interest is really in the December (1996) quarter and then following through into March to see where the turning point is going to be," said Stuart Marshall, economic analyst at Bancorp Treasury Services.
"We're picking that the slowdown through the year will end in the December quarter, so September will be a lot lower than the (annual) 2.6 percent we had in June.
"And we're picking that December will be slightly lower than September, but then March will pick up."
Economists said the GDP data were too historical to be of more than passing interest and only a very large rise or fall in the September quarter would kick the markets into action.
A very robust number could prompt a rise in interest rates and the New Zealand dollar, while a very weak number could have the opposite effect.
"Clearly if you get a negative number you might get a bit of reaction on the day, or if it was plus 1.0, but it will have to be a big number either way," Plank said.
